analysis.one_liner: Cuts the Pentagon budget by $100 billion, shielding troop pay and military health care.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Armed Services Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Barbara Lee's bill would have cut the Department of Defense's budget authority for fiscal year 2024 by $100 billion below what it spent in fiscal year 2023. It protected military health care, troop pay, and civilian federal employee pay from the cuts, targeting the rest of the Pentagon's budget instead. The bill also stated Congress's view that many urgent national security threats are not military, and that savings should go to other national priorities. It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, since the $100 billion in savings could be reallocated to non-military priorities like health care, education, or infrastructure. Military service members and DoD civilian employees would also be shielded from pay and benefit cuts, since the bill excludes those accounts from the reduction.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the amount authorized to be appropriated for the Department of Defense for fiscal year 2024 by $100 billion below the fiscal year 2023 level, with savings to be reallocated to other national priorities.
Excludes the Defense Health Program, military personnel accounts, and civil service pay and benefit accounts from the reductions, so troop pay and military health care are not cut.
Requires the Defense Secretary to consider the Congressional Budget Office's October 2021 report on operating under a smaller defense budget when implementing cuts.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors and weapons programs would see reduced funding. The Pentagon would lose budget authority for procurement, research and development, and other non-personnel accounts, which supporters of higher military spending argue could weaken readiness and deterrence.

drawbacks.text: Critics of large defense cuts argue that reducing the Pentagon budget could weaken military readiness and deterrence against rivals like China and Russia, and that the cuts land on weapons programs rather than overhead waste.

The bill never specified exactly which programs would be cut, deferring instead to a CBO menu of options, so the actual human and readiness costs of a $100 billion cut would depend entirely on later implementation choices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A $100 billion cut is large and the bill protected service members' pay and military health care from the reductions, but it left the specific program cuts to later decisions using a CBO options report, which made it a statement of priorities more than a ready-to-execute plan. The main practical cost would fall on weapons programs and defense contractors; the main risk is to military capability, though supporters argue much of the current budget addresses threats that are not primarily military in nature.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee in February 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Lee introduced the People Over Pentagon Act of 2023 on February 21, 2023, with 11 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the same day.
Ultimately 24 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee never acted on the bill, and it received no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors and the Pentagon's weapons procurement accounts are better off, since the $100 billion cut never happened. Members of Congress who favor higher defense spending avoided a recorded vote on reducing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors and Pentagon budget defenders

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the Pentagon budget by $100 billion for fiscal year 2024 while protecting military health care and personnel accounts.

for.name: 24 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats and the committee controlling the bill was never going to advance it under Republican or bipartisan support; the bill had no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: A $100 billion cut to the Pentagon budget would reduce funding for weapons procurement, research and development, and other programs that defense contractors sell into. The bill's death meant those contracts and revenue streams continued at prior funding levels.

industries.industry: Defense personnel and military health care
industries.note: The bill explicitly excluded the Defense Health Program, military personnel accounts, and civil service pay and benefits from the cuts, protecting service members' pay and military health care even while shrinking the rest of the budget.
